inline.caption: Arabic calligraphy on a page of a religious book. The Quran was recited in more than one accepted way from the Prophet's lifetime.
A folio of an early Quran in Hijazi script (Bibliothèque nationale de France, Arabe 334c): early copies lack the dots and vowel marks that later helped fix the readings.

inline.alt: An open Quran displayed on a wooden stand.
inline.caption: An open Quran on a stand. The accepted readings are the ones that reached the community by mass transmission.

inline.alt: Close view of Arabic calligraphy in a religious text.
inline.caption: Close view of Arabic script. A reading is accepted only if it fits the text of the copies, Arabic grammar and a sound chain.

inline.alt: Letterpress type and a pressure plate in a printing house.
inline.caption: Letterpress type. The Cairo edition of 1924 was a printing decision to follow one reading, and not a new text.
An elderly man washes for prayer at a fountain in an old courtyard in Kayseri, Türkiye. Washing comes before the Friday prayer.
An elderly man performs ablution at a mosque fountain, the step that comes before entering the prayer hall.

inline.alt: Aerial view of a large congregation praying inside an ornate mosque.
inline.caption: Worshippers pray in rows inside a large mosque. At the Friday prayer people stand shoulder to shoulder, in lines and not in pews.

inline.alt: A minaret of a mosque against a clear blue sky.
inline.caption: A minaret, from which the call to prayer is made before the Friday sermon.
A dirt road winding through a foggy forest. Muslims believe God knows the end of every path, and each person still walks it by choice.
An autumn forest in fog. Belief in qadar, God's decree, is one of the six articles of faith.

inline.alt: A path forking into two glowing roads in a forest, with a signpost.
inline.caption: A fork in the road. The Quran treats each person as responsible for the choice he makes.

inline.alt: The Milky Way over silhouetted trees at night.
inline.caption: The night sky. The Quran points to the order of creation as a sign that nothing is left to chance.
Antique coins on a wooden surface. The jizya was assessed in coin, in rates set by ability to pay.
A gold dinar of the caliph Abd al-Malik, minted in 697–98. The state's revenues and payments were reckoned in coin.

inline.alt: The Dome of the Rock and surrounding buildings in Jerusalem.
inline.caption: Jerusalem, called Aelia in the charter of ʿUmar, which set the terms of the jizya for its Christians in 15 AH.

inline.alt: The Damascus Gate and city wall of the Old City of Jerusalem.
inline.caption: The wall of Jerusalem's Old City. Muslim rulers owed protection to those who paid the jizya, and returned it when they could not give it.
The ceiling and windows of an old stone church. The Quran lists churches among the places where God's name is much remembered (22:40).
Candles burning in a church. The Quran says that among Christians are priests and monks who are not arrogant (5:82).

inline.alt: Saint Catherine's Monastery below the mountains of Sinai, Egypt.
inline.caption: Saint Catherine's Monastery in Sinai, one of the oldest Christian monasteries still in use, long under Muslim rule.

inline.alt: The Hanging Church, a Coptic Christian landmark in Cairo.
inline.caption: The Hanging Church in Cairo. Coptic Christians have worshipped in Egypt under Muslim rule since the seventh century.
Close-up of a laboratory microscope. The article grades each claim by what the evidence supports.
Microscopes on a laboratory table. A claim counts only as far as it can be tested.

inline.alt: Raindrops hitting a wet pavement and making ripples.
inline.caption: Raindrops. The Quran describes rain and the cycle of water, an accurate description, though not a unique one.

inline.alt: Depiction of the solar system with the sun and planets in a row.
inline.caption: The sun and planets. The Quran's verse on each body moving in its own orbit (21:33) is read as fair, and no more.
Volunteers hand out water and supplies outdoors. Islam joins worship to care for those in need.
Volunteers give food and aid to a man in a wheelchair. The Quran presses the duty to protect the weak.

inline.alt: A statue of Lady Justice holding scales.
inline.caption: Lady Justice with scales. The Quran asks for justice even against yourself, your parents and your relatives (4:135).

inline.alt: Close-up of an old hand and a young hand together.
inline.caption: Old and young hands. The Quran puts honour for parents next to the worship of God (17:23).
Three vintage hardbound books on a white surface. The Quran claims the same chain of prophets as the earlier scriptures.
A stack of old books on a table. Muslims and Christians share the names of many of the same prophets.

inline.alt: The interior of the Mosque-Cathedral of Córdoba, Spain.
inline.caption: The Mosque-Cathedral of Córdoba, a building shared by two faiths. Arabic-speaking Christians call God Allah.

inline.alt: Rays of light through clouds at sunrise.
inline.caption: Light through clouds. Islam holds that God is one and unlike creation, and the same God sent every prophet.
Aged vintage paper. Hadith were written down from the lifetime of the Prophet, not only handed on by memory.
An old parchment document. Muslim scholars checked written records against the memory of the narrators.

inline.alt: A quill, ink and paper on a desk.
inline.caption: A quill and ink on a desk. Writing began early, and scholars such as Ibn Sirin asked for the source of every report.

inline.alt: Black and white close-up of interlocking steel chains.
inline.caption: Interlocking chain links. An isnad is a chain of narrators, and each link was tested.
A vintage book, quill and ink holder on a wooden table. These seven scholars shaped how Islam's texts are written, read and studied.
A page of a manuscript of Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine. Scholars of the Islamic world wrote in medicine and philosophy as well as law and theology.

inline.alt: A man in a library holding books.
inline.caption: A reader in a library. Hunayn ibn Ishaq and others translated the works of earlier peoples into Arabic.

inline.alt: An open decorated Quran page.
inline.caption: An open Quran. Ibn Abbas, Abu Dawud, al-Ashʿarī and al-Ghazālī each shaped how the Quran, hadith and theology were studied.
A grand arched library hall. The Islamic world built great libraries in Baghdad, Cordoba, Cairo, Fez and Timbuktu.
A medieval illustration of scholars reading among shelves of books. These libraries held the works of earlier peoples and new work in Arabic.

inline.alt: A page of an old Arabic manuscript from Timbuktu.
inline.caption: A page from the Timbuktu manuscripts, held in the Library of Congress. West African libraries kept thousands of Arabic manuscripts.

inline.alt: The Süleymaniye Mosque and its minaret in Istanbul.
inline.caption: The Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul. Its complex houses the Süleymaniye Library, a large collection of Islamic manuscripts.
An antique Bible on a stand. Christians and Muslims read the same sayings of Jesus in the Gospel of John in different ways.
An open Bible at the Acts of the Apostles, in Spanish and English. How a verse is read depends on the passage around it.

inline.alt: A Holy Bible on a stand in a church.
inline.caption: A Bible on a church stand. Christians read John 1:1 as a statement that Jesus is God; Muslims point to the Quran's phrase "a word from Him" (3:45).

inline.alt: An open Quran with wooden prayer beads.
inline.caption: An open Quran with prayer beads. Muslims read these verses against the Quran's own account of Jesus as a prophet and servant of God.
A caravan of camels crossing the desert. Khadija was a merchant who sent caravans out with her goods.
A camel caravan at sunset. Aminah, the Prophet's mother, died on the road back from Medina when he was a small child.

inline.alt: Date palm trees under a clear blue sky.
inline.caption: Date palms. Mariya, the mother of Ibrahim, came from Egypt to the oasis city of Medina.

inline.alt: A woman holding an old book.
inline.caption: A woman with an old book. Aisha was among the most important transmitters of knowledge in her generation.
An old city gate lit at night. The Prophet made treaties with Jewish tribes in an oasis town of mixed tribes.
The ruined arches of an old building. The classical commentators read these verses against the history of earlier peoples.

inline.alt: The interior of a historic synagogue with carved wooden pews.
inline.caption: The interior of a synagogue. The Quran faults particular conduct and honours the upright among the People of the Book (3:113).
An old stone room with arched doorways. Classical jurists argued over the penalty for leaving the faith.
A half-open blue door in red light. The Quran says there is no compulsion in religion (2:256).

inline.alt: A dark room with a door slightly ajar and a line of light.
inline.caption: A door left ajar. Some modern scholars, including a Grand Mufti of Egypt, hold that leaving belief alone carries no worldly penalty.
Handwriting in elegant calligraphy. Algebra, algorithm and many other English words come from Arabic.
Arabic calligraphy in a religious text. Arabic gave English words through science as well as religion.

inline.alt: Copper distillery apparatus with shiny copper bowls.
inline.caption: Copper distillation apparatus. The alembic and the word alcohol (al-kuhl) entered European languages through Arabic chemistry.
The mud-brick ruins of Kharanaq in Iran. Salman came to Arabia from Persia.
Old mud-brick architecture in Iran, the land Salman al-Farisi left in search of the truth.

inline.alt: A town in the desert beneath mountains.
inline.caption: A town in the desert beneath mountains. Many of the first Muslims started with no wealth or standing.
Three crosses on a hill. The Quran answers the claim of those who said they killed the Messiah (4:157).
The Stone of Unction in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, a lithograph. Historians treat the crucifixion as well attested.

inline.alt: The Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
inline.caption: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, built over the traditional site of the crucifixion and burial of Jesus.
Tourbillon Castle in Sion, Switzerland, a medieval hilltop fortress. The word crusade is used far more widely than the history supports.
A medieval illustration of the Crusaders' conquest of Jerusalem in 1099.

inline.alt: The Sea Castle at Sidon on the coast of Lebanon.
inline.caption: The Sea Castle at Sidon (Saida) in Lebanon, a fortress that the Crusaders built on the coast in the thirteenth century.

inline.alt: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina in daylight.
inline.caption: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina, where the Prophet is buried. He warned against turning graves into places of worship.
